The 17th meeting of the Disarmament and International Security Committee, the first committee of the 80th session of the General Assembly, is called to order. The committee will now continue its thematic discussion under the cluster on outer space. Before I open the floor, I would like to inform delegations that 33 speakers remain on the list of speakers. Should the Committee complete consideration of the cluster this morning, as envisaged by the programme of work, in time permitting, we will immediately begin consideration of the cluster on other disarmament measures and international security, originally scheduled for this afternoon. The first speaker on the list of speakers is the His Excellency, the Permanent Representative of Guinea-Bissau, on behalf of the African Group.

Mr. Chairman, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the African Group. The Group aligns its statement with that of the Non-Aligned Movement to be delivered. The African Group reaffirms that outer space and celestial bodies constitute the common heritage of humankind and must be explored and utilized exclusively for peaceful purposes and for the benefit of all states irrespective of their level of development. The group emphasizes the urgency of preventing an arms race in outer space through a legally binding, multilaterally verifiable instrument consistent with the principles of non-appropriation, and peaceful use as enshrined in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty and related UN instruments. We welcome the adoption of General Assembly resolutions 79/19, 79/20 and 79/51, which collectively reaffirm the importance of maintaining outer space for peaceful purposes, transparency, and confidence-building among States. The Group also welcomes the establishment of the new Open-ended Working Group on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, pursuant to GA decision 79/512, and encourages continued progress in its work. The African Group reiterates that outer space must remain free of nuclear weapons, weapons of mass destruction, and all other forms of armament whose presence threatens international peace and security and the survival of humanity. We further stress strict compliance with all existing disarmament and arms limitation obligations relevant to outer space. Mr. Chairman, The group calls for the early commencement of substantive negotiation in the Conference on Disarmament on a legally binding instrument on pyros, building on the recommendation of the Group of Governmental Experts established pursuant to Resolution 77/250. The African Group underscored the importance of international cooperation, capacity building, and equal access to outer space technologies. In this regard, we highlight the African space policy and strategy adopted under Agenda 2063 and the establishment of the African Space Agency as milestones towards enhancing Africa's peaceful participation in outer space. The group expresses deep concern over the intentional creation of space debris through deliberate destruction of space systems, which poses a serious threat to the sustainability of outer space activities. We therefore call for measures to mitigate and prohibit such action while ensuring that developing countries are not deprived of opportunity to build peaceful space capabilities and bridge the digital divide. Finally, the African Group reaffirms transparency, confidence-building measures remain vital for preserving outer space as a domain of peace, security, and sustainable development for all humanity. Thank you.
I thank the Ambassador of Guinea-Bissau for his statement on behalf of African Group. You now have the floor to the distinguished representative of New Zealand.

Chair, in 2024, New Zealand hosted the third highest number of orbital launches worldwide. We take our responsibilities as a launching state seriously. We are committed to ensuring that space activity taking place in New Zealand is conducted safely, responsibly, and sustainably. We believe outer space must be governed in a way that reflects the international community's collective interests and responsibilities. This includes ensuring that all states, regardless of size or capability, can participate meaningfully in shaping the future of space governance. We remain committed to reducing the risk of conflict in space, particularly through the development of norms, rules, and principles of responsible behavior. We also contribute to efforts to apply international space law to emerging activities, such as debris removal and on-orbit servicing, work that is essential to maintaining a safe and sustainable space environment. New Zealand welcomes the momentum generated by recent multilateral processes, especially the success of open-ended working groups on responsible behaviors and on the prevention of an arms race in outer space. It is essential that we continue to deepen our shared understanding and build convergence on key issues, including the applicability of international law, including international humanitarian law, to outer space activities, the protection of space systems that deliver critical civilian services, or those critical to preservation of international security. The importance of transparency and information sharing to support the development of future legally binding instruments. Chair, we remain concerned by proposals that risk fragmenting the multilateral space security architecture or creating disproportionate challenges for smaller states. Despite encouraging progress, New Zealand remains deeply concerned about activities that could jeopardize the safe and predictable use of outer space. We reiterate our call for all states to abide by their international commitments stemming from the Outer Space Treaty. New Zealand recognizes the valuable role of COPUOS in supporting an effective international legal framework that enables the growth of the global space sector and facilitates international cooperation. New Zealand will continue to champion an inclusive and multi-stakeholder approach to space governance in an effort to build a space environment that is safe and sustainable for the benefit of all. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of New Zealand for her statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. Chair, the Russian Federation has consistently been calling for keeping outer space as a heritage for all mankind and for making sure it's used exclusively for peaceful purpose. The only way of achieving the goal of PAROS in outer space is only through the development of comprehensive, legally binding principles and norms of international law, and they ought to be comprehensive in nature. We note with regret and concern that these values are not shared by all Member States. We witness a growing risk of turning outer space into a platform for aggression and war. A number of Western states openly pursue the course towards placing weapons in outer space and using outer space for combat operations to guarantee their dominance and superiority. A good example here is the US efforts on the Golden Dome for America project. It involves a comprehensive development of components of the global missile defense system, including the orbital deployment of interceptors. Such actions are putting at serious risk the long-term sustainability of peaceful outer space activities, can destabilize the situation, and will lead to an arms race in outer space. At the present stage, however, it's still feasible to prevent a full-scale arms race in outer space. UN member states should, for this, undertake obligations not to place weapons of any kind in outer space and ban the threat or use of force against any space objects or involving them. It's important to establish a comprehensive ban on space strike weapons designed to destroy outer space object. there is a basis for launching the negotiation on this. I'm referring to the updated draft of PPWT and the consensual report of GGE on PAROS of 2024. On this basis, it is necessary to continue work on substantive elements of relevant international legal binding instrument here. We are satisfied with the start of the substantive discussion within the Open-Ended Working Group on PAROS. which was established by United Nations Decision 79/512. It is necessary to ensure that its work is constructive and politicized if we want to achieve tangible results on the basis of adopted modalities. We believe that any non-binding measures, including TCBMs, should complement but not substitute effective legally binding instruments on Paris. What remains very much in demand is the international initiative, political commitment of no first placement of weapons in outer space. We call on UN member states to globalize this, to universalize this initiative and to undertake political commitments in this regard. The full 37 countries are already members of this initiative. Mr. Chairman, the Russian Federation is submitting three draft resolutions on space issues for the consideration of the first committee, and we're calling on all states to speak in support and co-sponsor them. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Russian Federation for his statement. Again, on the floor, the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Malaysia associates itself with the statements by NAM and by ASEAN. As technological advances open new doors for exploration, we must not lose sight of the need to protect outer space from the dangers of militarization. Maintaining the use of outer space for exclusively peaceful purposes is imperative, especially in times of rising tension and major power rivalry. Malaysia recognizes the indispensable role of inclusive multilateral discourse regarding outer space. It's important that we collectively avoid institutional fragmentation and ensure the equitable participation of all states in expounding and further developing the applicable rules, norms, and principles in this domain. My delegation welcomes the adoption of the agenda and indicative program of work of the Open-Ended Working Group on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space in all its aspects, 2024 to 2028. This is an encouraging signal of the political will of the global community in preserving outer space as a common heritage of mankind, which we should build upon as the OEWG advances its substantive deliberations. the same spirit my delegation also recalls last year's adoption by consensus of the final report of the group of governmental experts of further measures to prevent an arms race in outer space pursuant to General Assembly resolution 77250 Mr chair in January 2025 the Malaysian spaceport act 2022 fully entered into force ensuring a robust legal framework for the regulation of our national space activities and the fulfilment of relevant international obligations. On 26 September 2025, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Malaysia deposited our instrument of accession to the Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space, thereby effecting its entry into force for Malaysia. Subsequently, on the 21st of October, Malaysia submitted its instrument of ratification for the Outer Space Treaty of 1967. These measures reflect Malaysia's aspiration to become an active and responsible player in the rapidly growing global space sector, including through adherence to foundational instruments of international space law. Malaysia also commends the continued efforts of the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, given the critical role of capacity building in this field, particularly for developing countries. I thank you, Mr Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Bangladesh.

Thank you, Chair. Bangladesh aligns itself with the statement delivered by Indonesia on behalf of the NAM. In addition, allow me to present our position. Bangladesh expresses deep concern regarding the threats to international peace and security by the possible weaponization of outer space. armed conflict in space would make the entire domain a battlefield and jeopardize international peace and security. We underscore that the exploration and use of outer space should exclusively be for peaceful purposes only. Bangladesh firmly believes that access to outer space is an inalienable right of all states and recognize outer space as a global common for the entire humanity beyond the jurisdiction of any one state. With this commitment, we proudly join the committee on the peaceful uses of outer space. As a State Party to the Outer Space Treaty, we reaffirm the vital importance of preventing arms race in outer space. We reiterate our call that all activities in the outer space must be done in accordance with international law and the principle of non-appropriation of outer space. Mr. Chair, the outer space environment has been significantly impacted by the growing number of space objects. The distinction between peaceful and military applications of outer space has become increasingly blurred. This highlights the urgent need to strengthen the current legal framework and security aspects of outer space to address the emerging threats. Bangladesh re-emphasizes the urgent need for the commencement of substantive negotiation in the Conference on Disarmament on a legally binding and multilaterally verifiable instrument on the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. We emphasize the necessity for improved information sharing regarding the purpose of space objects, the intentions behind operations, and the corresponding mechanisms. We urge States not to use any space or ground-based capabilities, including anti-satellite. whether exclusively military or multi-use, to deliberately damage or destroy space assets. We call on space-faring nations to respect applicable laws and norms on the use of weapons in outer space and develop appropriate and effective instruments that will prevent an arms race in outer space. Bangladesh underscores that activities in outer space must not remain the exclusive preserve of a small group of States. We call for strengthening of capacity-building programmes, with particular emphasis on developing countries, to ensure that outer space is, both in principle and in practice, a truly global commons which all States can avail themselves to. To conclude, the exploration and use of outer space must be carried out only for the benefit of all humankind and in the interest of all countries. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Bangladesh for his statement. We now have the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore.

Thank you, Mr Chair. Singapore aligns itself with the statements delivered by Laos on behalf of ASEAN and Indonesia on behalf of NAM. We would like to offer three additional points in our national capacity. First, outer space should remain a peaceful global commons that is accessible to all humankind. No state should appropriate outer space by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means. We must continue to uphold a rules-based approach to outer space governance based on international law, including the 1967 Outer Space Treaty and other relevant international law. Singapore supports practical approaches towards shaping a common framework for outer space security, whether through the development of norms of responsible behaviours in outer space or a legally binding and verifiable instrument in the future. We view both types of measures as complementary and encourage all states to engage in constructive conversations moving forward. Second, we must take concrete steps to facilitate open and effective communication between spacefaring nations. We encourage all Member States to build on achieved consensus, such as the 2013 GGE on transparency and confidence-building measures in outer space activities, and the 2024 GGE on further practical measures for PAROS. Singapore supports the conduct of outer space activities in a transparent manner. including in proximity operations, where advance notification should be provided to the extent practicable. While such operations may be conducted for peaceful purposes, they may be misinterpreted by others and lead to unintended escalations. Third, discussions on outer space must be conducted in an inclusive manner. We welcome the progress towards substantive and constructive discussions at the second substantive session of the OEWG on PAROS in all its aspects in July this year.

To do our part,

Singapore, together with Australia and the UN Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific, organized two virtual capacity building workshops for regional member states earlier this year, which we hope will encourage greater participation from delegations in outer space security discussions. To conclude, Singapore reaffirms our commitment to work constructively with all Member States on preserving outer space as a sustainable, secure and stable environment for the benefit of humanity. Thank you. Our full statement has been uploaded in the interest of time.
I thank the representative of Singapore for her statement. We now have the floor to the distinguished representative of Algeria.

Mr. Chair, Algeria aligns itself with the statements delivered on behalf of NAM, the African Group, and the Arab Group. We recognize outer space as a common heritage of mankind and the inalienable sovereign rights of all states to explore and use it exclusively for peaceful purposes, benefiting all states irrespective of their development levels. We express serious concerns over the threats from possible weaponization of outer space. Preventing an arms race in outer space is imperative for international peace and security and must be addressed holistically through legally binding instruments, our priority that cannot be delayed or substituted. We welcome decision 79/512, establishing the Open-Ended Working Group on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, or PAROS, and call for constructive engagement to consolidate UN discussions and avoid duplication. The Conference on Disarmament, as a sole multilateral negotiating forum, must establish a dedicated powers organ to negotiate prohibition of any weapons deployment and attacks against space objects. The Russia-China draft treaty constitutes a solid negotiating basis in this regard. We emphasize strict compliance with existing agreements, particularly the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while developing frameworks for new challenges. Transparency and confidence-building measures are important complementary steps, but cannot substitute for legally binding instruments. We call upon States, especially those with major space capabilities, to contribute actively to peaceful uses and refrain from contrary actions. We express concern over activities threatening space security and call for restraint and transparency. We emphasize strengthening international cooperation based on equality and non-discrimination, per the Declaration on International Cooperation in Outer Space. Finally, developing countries must benefit equitably through capacity building, technology transfer, and information exchange without discriminatory restrictions. Any regulatory arrangements must not impede legitimate peaceful uses. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the representative of Algeria for his statement. I give now the floor to His Excellency, Permanent Representative of Myanmar.

Thank you, Chair. Myanmar aligns itself with the statement of ASEAN and NAM. Mr. Chair, peaceful uses of outer space and space systems, including space technology, satellites, and space-based communications are indispensable to humanity. Myanmar reaffirms that access to outer space as an inalienable right of all states and its use for exclusively peaceful purposes. In this context, we underscore the importance of strengthening international cooperation and capacity building to assist the developing countries with their equitable access to outer space for peaceful use and sustainable development. As part of our initiation of its peaceful use, Myanmar collaborated with Japan on our first satellite development program under the elected civilian government. Directly developed by Myanmar Aerospace Engineering University and Hokkaido University, the first microsatellite of Myanmar was designed to provide real-time images for disaster risk management and monitoring agriculture, forestry, and fisheries. Unfortunately, the deployment was put on hold after the illegal military coup due to the growing concern over its military applications by the hunter. In this regard, Myanmar commends the preemptive approach taken by the government of Japan to prevent any misuse and appropriations of space technology by military hunter against civilians. Mr. Chair, we have witnessed time after time that the military hunters blur the lines between the duality of any good, from space technology, jet fuel, to even recreational paramotors at the expense of civilians. For the military hunter, the military aspect of dual-use item and the technologies always eclipses the civilian aspect as long as they can be utilized for their widespread terror campaign and systematic subjugation of civilian populations. Against this backdrop, we are seriously concerned that some Member States with major space-faring capabilities have enhanced their space technology cooperation with the military hunter, including a satellite imagery analysis centre under the guise of peaceful purposes. It is reported that the said Member State had offered to share information captured by its reconnaissance satellites with the hunter for military purposes. From 1 August to 23 October this year, the junta has conducted 348 airstrikes against civilians, killing 357 people. Therefore, I appeal to all Member States to cut the flow of arms, weapons, jet fuel and other dual-use items and related technologies to the military junta to save the lives of the people of Myanmar. I thank you, Mr Chair.
I thank the Ambassador. Myanmar for his statement. Now the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Chair. Today we face an accelerating arms race and creeping weaponization of outer space. Outer space is increasingly being framed as the next war fighting domain, extending concepts of nuclear and conventional deterrence beyond Earth. The intertwining of defensive and offensive capabilities, such as missile defense systems integrated with space technologies, is eroding strategic stability. The once hypothetical placement of interceptors in space is now being seriously pursued. The rapid development of anti-satellite directed energy and other non-kinetic weapons compounds these dangers. The line between peaceful and military uses of outer space is also blurring. Existing international space law, while valuable, has not effectively prevented the arms race or the weaponization of outer space. Recognizing these gaps, the international community has repeatedly called for further measures and appropriate international negotiations. It is imperative that space law evolve in step with technological and strategic realities. Confidence building and voluntary measures can complement but never replace legally binding obligations. Political convenience must not override the urgent need for comprehensive international agreements. Pakistan advocates a holistic approach, addressing both dual use concerns and explicitly military capabilities. A framework that integrates capabilities and behaviors offers the most credible pathway forward as shown by precedents in other disarmament regimes. The need for concrete, meaningful action is now more urgent than ever. Pakistan has consistently called for negotiations on a legally binding instrument while supporting the PPWT initiative. We also continue to contribute towards non-binding initiatives, such as transparency and confidence-building measures. We recognize their complementary nature. yet they cannot serve as a substitute or a precondition for them. In the open-ended working group on PAROS in all its aspects, we have a unique opportunity to bridge differences and lay the foundation for future legally and non-legally binding measures. We welcome the agreement on organizational modalities that have enabled us to begin substantive work. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the representative of Pakistan for his statement. I give now the floor to Her Excellency, Permanent Representative of Japan to the Conference on Disarmament.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. There is a new urgency for effective measures to ensure security, stability, safety, and sustainability of activities in outer space for current and future generations. This year, the open-ended working group on the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects began its deliberations in Geneva. Japan reiterates the importance of inclusive, holistic, and comprehensive dialogues with multi-stakeholder engagement. Particularly, Japan strongly supports the continuation of discussions on reducing space threats, through norms, rules, and principles of responsible behavior. Japan considers this approach a practical way forward in advancing the prevention of an arms race in outer space, PAROS, in a concrete and practical manner, which enables us to avoid misperception, mistrust, and miscommunication among actors in space. Japan as one of the leading space-faring nations, remains firmly committed to the objective of PAROS and actively contribute to discussions aimed at promoting the development of international norms and rules for the use of outer space. Mr. Chair, with a view to making progress in our consideration of the issues related to outer space, Japan underscores the importance of the Outer Space Treaty once again as the cornerstone of the international legal framework for this critical domain. It is vital to reaffirm compliance with existing legal obligations, deepen understanding of the current state in outer space, and take a concrete and pragmatic step from there. We believe that reducing serious risks and threats posed by destabilizing space activities through norms, rules, and principles is the starting point for establishing an effective normative and legal framework that truly serves the objective of PAROS. Mr. Chair, Japan also underlines the importance of the Conference on Disarmament, the sole multilateral forum for negotiation on disarmament. We hope to generate synergy among various multilateral fora to facilitate dialogues among states and with other relevant stakeholders to foster common understandings and collective actions. This will enable our future generations to benefit from innovation, international collaboration, and remarkable technological achievement. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Ireland.

Chair, Ireland aligns with the statement delivered by the European Union. Ireland is firmly committed to the prevention of an arms race in outer space and to the preservation of a safe, secure and sustainable environment. Outer space must be used exclusively for peaceful purposes and on an equitable basis for the benefit of all humankind. Satellites and other space-based systems underpin our global economy and essential civilian infrastructure and contribute towards the achievement of the sustainable development goals. All states, spacefaring or otherwise, share a responsibility to strengthen the safety, security, and sustainability of outer space activities. Chair, Ireland reiterates opposition to the placement of any weapons in outer space. The development, deployment or testing of nuclear or other weapons in orbit would pose a catastrophic risk to satellites, to global communications and to the functioning of modern societies. We recall the obligations of the Outer Space Treaty and underscore the importance of preserving outer space as a domain free from weaponisation. Ireland is deeply concerned by the development and proliferation of anti-satellite weapons, whether space-based or terrestrial, which are a matter of humanitarian concern. Ireland supports a comprehensive approach within the multilateral system to address these weapons systems. Chair, as a global commons, outer space requires global governance. The development of rules, norms and principles of responsible behaviour grounded in existing international law including the UN Charter, international humanitarian law, and the principal UN space treaties, is essential to Ireland. Achieving the prevention of an arms race in outer space and a safe and secure outer space requires both legal measures and non-binding norms of behavior. This is a complementary approach. Such norms often serve to develop legal instruments and further strengthen them. While Ireland sees value in the eventual negotiation of legally binding instruments, We consider voluntary, pragmatic measures to be necessary and achievable. These should be developed through a transparent, multilateral and multi-stakeholder process. Ireland welcomes the commencement of the substantive work of the Open-ended Working Group on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space in all its aspects. We call on all States to engage constructively in this forum, which allows for consideration of legally binding and political commitments on an equal footing, in accordance with the Group's mandate. Finally, Chair, Ireland underlines the importance of engaging all relevant stakeholders, including international organizations, commercial actors, civil society, academia, and the ICRC, in strengthening space security and ensuring the peaceful and sustainable use of outer space for generations.
I thank the representative of Ireland for your statement. Now the floor to the distinguished representative of Sweden.

Thank you, Chair.

Sweden fully aligns itself with the statement made by the European Union.

The following remarks are made in my national capacity.

A rules-based world order and multilateralism are essential for a safe, secure, and sustainable space environment. Global challenges, such as increasing space threats, require a collective approach to deliver effective and trustworthy solutions. Societies rely heavily on space for essential services, space is becoming increasingly congested and contested. We need appropriate measures to reduce threats and avoid conflict. Chair, the first step to strengthen space security is full compliance by all states with

existing international law, including the UN Charter.

The Outer Space Treaty is the cornerstone of the international legal regime governing outer space activities. We urge all States to fully comply with its obligations, including its Article IV, not to place in orbit any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other weapons of mass destruction. Last year's resolution affirmed this key arms control obligation and urged States not to develop capabilities for such purposes. Outer space must remain free from weapons of mass destruction.

Chair,

As an example of the challenges we face, I'd like to mention the steep increase in the number of harmful global navigation satellite systems interferences in the Baltic Sea region. This affects civil aviation, the maritime sector, as well as critical infrastructure and other services. Sweden recalls that under the Outer Space Treaty's Article 9, States Parties shall conduct all their activities in outer space with due regard to the corresponding interests of all other States Parties to the Treaty.

Chair, we are convinced that space security can be strengthened through a variety of actions, political and legally binding measures.

We should work to reduce risks and threats, including by advancing efforts on responsible space behavior. We should strengthen the implementation of existing international legal and normative frameworks.

Like many other countries, Sweden has committed not to conduct destructive direct

ascent anti-satellite missile tests and urges all states to make such a commitment.

An inclusive forum with participation of all stakeholders increases the chances of success.

Sweden welcomes that the open-ended working group on prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects is finally up and running.

As space threats increase, so does the urgency for global cooperation to address them.

I thank you.
I thank the representative of Sweden for his statement. I give now the floor to His Excellency, Permanent Representative of Iraq.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. We associate ourselves with the statement of the Sultanate of Oman on behalf of the Arab Group and the statement of Indonesia on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. Mr. Chair. Iraq reiterates that outer space is a common heritage for all humankind and must be explored for exclusively peaceful purposes and that it must be accessible to everyone. We fully support all initiatives aimed at enhancing the peaceful and just use of outer space for everyone. At the same time, we reaffirm the need to consolidate these initiatives in order for member states to be able to have an inclusive discussion and to adopt one coherent path in order to enhance international efforts to prevent the militarization of outer space and to prevent an arms race in it to reach our final objective, which is securing an outer space that is safe and secure for us and future generations. In this context, we welcome the adoption of the final report of the GGE on the practical measures for preventing an arms race in the outer space, which provides a number of core elements for a legally binding international instrument, including preventing the placement of weapons in space and enhancing transparency and confidence-building measures and suitable verification mechanisms. In conclusion, we reiterate the need to avoid a conflict between the paths and initiatives for preventing an arms race in outer space. We support the current efforts to consolidate these paths, to support collective action to achieve a space, an outer space that is secure and safe and free of any military activities. Thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador of Iraq, for your statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Thank you, Chair. Despite being on the agendas of the UN General Assembly and of the CD for over 40 years, the issue of the prevention of an arms race in outer space remains critically underdeveloped. This persistent deadlock is further exacerbated by the exponential increase in tensions linked to the use of the space environment. Brazil remains deeply concerned about the impact that the weaponization of outer space would have on international security and on the current and future uses of space for peaceful purposes. The issue of powers and outer space security also has a direct relationship with a strategic competition in the nuclear domain and therefore influences perspectives for nuclear disarmament. However, the discussions on the topic throughout 2025 present an opportunity for renewed optimism. Last year, on the initiative of the core group of countries, including my own, the General Assembly adopted a decision to merge the two separate open-ended working groups on space security and powers, avoiding duplication of efforts and the escalation of political divisions. Despite the challenges initially presented, the OEWG on powers in all its aspects successfully initiated its substantive work. Brazil thanks the efforts made by the chair of the group, Ambassador Carlos Mario Foradori of Argentina. In this regard, the group's unified and comprehensive approach proved to be the most effective strategy for advancing the topic. Chair, Brazil remains committed to negotiating a legally binding instrument on powers and believes that the current adoption of non-binding confidence-building measures, rules and principles of behavior should contribute to enhancing the existing legal framework and building trust. Within the framework of PAROS in all its aspects, we expect the OEWG to consider all vectors of space threats identified in recent multilateral discussions, especially in the consensus report adopted by last year's GGE on PAROS. The placement of weapons in outer space and the development of counter space capabilities against such weapons are mutually reinforcing issues, which equally require the urgent attention of the international community. Growing tensions in space impair the sustainability of peaceful uses of outer space, which is of critical importance for all countries, regardless of their domestic technological capabilities. If not halted, the trend towards the weaponization of outer space risks eroding international cooperation in this domain disproportionate impact on developing countries. Pending concrete progress in strengthening the bilateral framework for space security in Paris, our main responsibility remains to uphold the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. Its key provisions, the prohibiting placing of nuclear weapons, is more vital today, given the critical role of space assets for all states. Thank you.
Thank you, representative of Brazil, for your statement. Now the floor to the distinguished representative of Maldives.

Thank you, Chair. The Maldives aligns with the statement delivered by Nauru and reaffirms its commitment to the peaceful exploration and use of outer space for the benefit and in the interest of all humankind. Outer space must remain a global common, governed by cooperation and transparency. Legal instruments alone cannot ensure this. It requires responsible behaviour, mutual trust and the capacity of all States, including Small Island Developing States, to contribute to and benefit from the peaceful use of space. The Maldives welcomes the report of Secretary-General on outer space security. The accelerating developments of counter space capabilities and the absence of agreed norms governing their use remains cause for deep concerns. Preventing an arm race in outer space depends on responsible behavior, transparency and trust, the foundation of any treaty governing outer space. For small island developing states, outer space is the next new frontier. For SIDS, it is a vital tool for survival and development. Space-based data hold transformative possibilities For climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction and ocean resources management, SIDS can also use such data to better preserve, protect and monitor their vast EEZs and maritime biodiversity. As we chart As humanity's path beyond the horizon, we must ensure that outer space becomes a horizon of resilience, a promise of shared progress. The Maldives proposes three priorities for safer demilitarization and inclusive orbit. First, add a practical transparency and confidence building measures, including shared situational awareness data and incident prevention to reduce risk and miscalculation. Second, ensure seats and other developing countries have an increasing and meaningful role in multilateral forums and frameworks relating to shape long-term norms and rules of space conduct while strengthening UN Office for Outer Space Affairs and Committee on Peaceful Use of Outer Space as an inclusive, depoliticized platforms for cooperation. Third, critical gaps exist and must be bridged through strengthened international cooperation in the exchange of satellite data, the extension of emergency connectivity to vulnerable regions, and the stewardship of transparent and sustainable space environment. Progress in space must serve humanity, advancing technology that protects lives and strengthens resilience and upholds shared security. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Maldives for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Philippines.

Thank you, Chair. We align ourselves with the statements delivered by Lao PDR on behalf of ASEAN and Indonesia on behalf of the NAM. The security and sustainability of outer space is a highly important aspect of global discourse. As technological advancement accelerates, states increasingly rely on space-based technologies for infrastructure, communications, navigation, weather forecasting, and disaster response. The Philippines relies on outer space for critical areas such as climate change and telecommunications, among others. As an emerging space actor, we see the need to update the governance framework for outer space. geopolitical rivalries and strategic competition risk transforming outer space into a theater of militarization and conflict. The current regime, anchored by the UN Charter and the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while relevant, is no longer sufficient to address the complexities of modern space activities in a possible arms race. We reaffirm that political commitments on responsible behaviors can be developed in support of and without prejudice to the pursuit of legally binding measures and instruments in outer space. These are not mutually exclusive. We emphasize the legal concept of due regard enshrined in the OST and also found in UN clause in the Chicago Convention as a key principle that ensures balance between established and emerging space actors, which could inform future negotiations on both legally binding instruments and norms of responsible behavior. We strongly support the streamlined discussions of the open-ended working group on Pyros in all its aspects, as evident in a joint statement led by the Philippines during the first session of the OEWG. Moreover, we support confidence-building measures such as the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation, particularly in the exchange of pre-launch notifications for space launch vehicles and their test flights to mitigate risk of accidents, especially those involving civilian aviation and maritime shipping.
